content:
Christian preachers often put the case to Muslims this way: every child of Adam is born guilty, under a sin it did not commit, and Islam, by denying it, cannot see why humanity needs a saviour. Muslim writers often answer that Augustine invented the doctrine in the fifth century.[1]

Both statements claim too much. The doctrine has an older history than Augustine, and it means different things in the Catholic, Orthodox and Reformed churches. The Quran, for its part, tells of Adam's sin in some detail, and of what followed it.

This article aims to provide context to the claim, insha'Allah, in six questions about original sin, each answered from the text it rests on. The Quran's frame is plain: "Every soul draws the meed of its acts on none but itself: no bearer of burdens can bear the burden of another" (6:164).[2]

Genesis 2 and 3 tell of the command, the eating and the expulsion, and name the consequences: pain in childbirth, labour, and death. "By the sweat of your face will you eat bread until you return to the ground" (Genesis 3:19).[3]

The chapter has no sentence saying that Adam's guilt passes to each of his descendants. The Torah elsewhere states the opposite principle for human justice: "The fathers shall not be put to death for the children, neither shall the children be put to death for the fathers" (Deuteronomy 24:16). Ezekiel makes it a principle of God's own judgement: "The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father" (Ezekiel 18:20).[4]

Christian theologians reply that original sin is something other than one father's offence charged to an unrelated son. That reply concedes the point at issue: the doctrine is built from later readings, and the Hebrew Bible does not state it.

The doctrine's main text is Romans 5:12: "Therefore as sin entered into the world through one man, and death through sin; and so death passed to all men, because all sinned." Verse 19 adds: "as through the one man's disobedience many were made sinners, even so through the obedience of the one, many will be made righteous."[5]

The question is what passed from Adam. The verse names death, and ties it to the sins that "all sinned". The Latin translation known to Augustine rendered the last clause as "in whom all sinned", which made Adam the one in whom all sinned. Augustine built on that reading, and modern translations, including the Catholic ones, have corrected it.[6]

He did not invent it. Cyprian of Carthage, writing in 251 or 252 with sixty-six bishops, defended the baptism of newborn infants on the ground that an infant "has not sinned, except in that, being born after the flesh according to Adam, he has contracted the contagion of the ancient death at its earliest birth". What is remitted to him in baptism, Cyprian says, is "not his own sins, but the sins of another".[7]

Pier Franco Beatrice argues that a doctrine of inherited sin was already widespread in the West before Augustine, with roots in second-century Egypt. Augustine's achievement, on his account, was to unite the strands into the form the Latin church made orthodox in the controversy with Pelagius.[8]

The Muslim reply, then, is better put this way: the doctrine took shape over three centuries after Jesus (peace be upon him), from a reading of Paul, and none of its formulations is found in the words of Jesus.

They do not. The Catechism of the Catholic Church calls original sin a sin "contracted" and not "committed", a state and not an act, and says that in Adam's descendants it "does not have the character of a personal fault"; it is a deprivation of original holiness and justice.[9]

The Orthodox Church in America teaches that humanity inherits the consequences of Adam's sin, chiefly death, and not his personal guilt, and many Orthodox writers prefer the term "ancestral sin".[10] The Westminster Confession, at the other end, says that the guilt of Adam's sin "was imputed" to all his posterity, together with a corrupted nature.[11]

A Muslim answer has to say which doctrine it answers. To the Reformed confession, the Quran's reply is 6:164. With the Catholic and Orthodox churches the question shifts from guilt to the state in which a child is born.

Infant baptism tied the doctrine to the life of every family. The Catholic Catechism teaches that children are born with a fallen nature and need the new birth of baptism, which takes away original sin, while its consequences remain.[12] Cyprian's letter shows the same reasoning in the third century.[7]

The practice divides the churches themselves. Baptists and many other Protestant communities baptise only those old enough to profess faith, so they reject the practice that did most to spread the doctrine.

The Quran agrees that Adam disobeyed: "thus did Adam disobey his Lord, and allow himself to be seduced" (20:121). It goes on in the next verse: "But his Lord chose him (for His Grace): He turned to him, and gave him Guidance" (20:122).[2]

Adam and his wife repent together: "Our Lord! We have wronged our own souls: If thou forgive us not and bestow not upon us Thy Mercy, we shall certainly be lost" (7:23). "Then learnt Adam from his Lord words of inspiration, and his Lord turned towards him" (2:37).[2] The sin is confessed, forgiven and closed within Adam's own life.

The Prophet (peace be upon him) said that every child is born upon the fiṭra, the natural disposition toward God, and that it is the parents who make the child a Jew, a Christian or a Magian.[13] The Quran calls that disposition "the pattern on which He has made mankind" (30:30).[2] Ismāʿīl al-Fārūqī put the Islamic position in one phrase: man begins "ethically sane and sound, not weighed down by any original sin".[14]

The bottom line

Genesis records Adam's sin and its consequences, and the Torah and Ezekiel deny that guilt passes from father to son. Paul linked Adam to the death of all; a Latin mistranslation and Augustine made him the one in whom all sinned; and the churches still differ on what was passed on. The doctrine is a work of interpretation, built over three centuries.

The Quran tells the same story with another end. Adam sins, repents and is forgiven; each child is born upon the fiṭra; and each soul answers for its own deeds, for "man can have nothing but what he strives for" (53:39).[2] A child born with no debt needs no one to pay it. Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. Both positions are common in popular Christian and Muslim debate; the Malay article Adakah Munasabah? in the Bismikaa archive is one example of the second.
  2. Quran 6:164; 20:121 to 122; 7:23; 2:37; 30:30; 53:38 to 39, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  3. Genesis 2:15 to 3:24 (World English Bible).
  4. Deuteronomy 24:16; Ezekiel 18:1 to 20 (World English Bible).
  5. Romans 5:12 to 21; 1 Corinthians 15:22 (World English Bible).
  6. On the Latin in quo omnes peccaverunt and its correction, see Joseph A. Fitzmyer, Romans, Anchor Bible 33 (New York: Doubleday, 1993), on Romans 5:12.
  7. Cyprian, Epistle 58 (64 in the Oxford numbering), To Fidus, on the Baptism of Infants 5, in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 5.
  8. Pier Franco Beatrice, The Transmission of Sin: Augustine and the Pre-Augustinian Sources, trans. Adam Kamesar (New York: Oxford University Press, 2013).
  9. Catechism of the Catholic Church, 404 to 405.
  10. Orthodox Church in America, "St. Augustine & Original Sin", in Questions and Answers.
  11. Westminster Confession of Faith (1646), chapter 6, section 3.
  12. Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1250 and 1263 to 1264.
  13. Sahih al-Bukhari 1359 and 4775 (numbering of sunnah.com); Sahih Muslim 2658.
  14. Ismāʿīl Rājī al-Fārūqī, Al Tawhid: Its Implications for Thought and Life, 2nd ed. (Herndon, VA: International Institute of Islamic Thought, 1992), chapter 1.
